title: The Earth hums
hook: The whole planet rings with a faint, endless hum far too low to hear.
peek: Seismometers show that the Earth is never quite still. Even on days with no earthquakes, the planet vibrates with a constant hum, thousands of times too low for human ears, mostly driven by ocean waves pounding the seafloor.
lede: After a very large earthquake the whole Earth rings like a bell for days, swelling and shrinking in slow vibrations that take minutes each. Scientists long assumed the ringing stopped between big quakes. In 1998 researchers in Japan, studying years of records from sensitive instruments, reported that it never does. The planet hums all the time.

bullets.text: The hum's vibrations take several minutes each, at roughly 2 to 7 thousandths of a cycle per second. Human hearing starts at about 20 cycles per second, so the hum is thousands of times too low to hear.

Most researchers now trace the hum to the oceans. Long, slow swells from storms press on the seafloor near coasts. In 2004 a study found it comes mostly from the northern oceans in northern winter and the southern oceans in southern winter.
The hum was first measured on land. In 2017 a team in France reported recording it with seismometers placed on the floor of the Indian Ocean, which may help map the Earth's interior.
